close_reason: Fixed in commit 00cd261. Flipped filter_changes_array's not-in-lookup branch from return false (drop) to return true (keep). Per-function rustdoc now documents the TOCTOU policy and the trade with backends that override get_metadata_changes. Added regression test changes_filter_keeps_id_when_object_disappeared_mid_flight that seeds two Ids in the change log with only one's Metadata in the mock store — both Ids survive the filter pass. All 32 tests pass; clippy clean.
description:
metadata.rs:228-247 — filter_changes_array is the default-impl post-filter path for Metadata/changes. It calls get_objects::<Metadata>(...ids_for_fetch...) and then filters:

    let Some(meta) = lookup.get(id_str) else {
        return false; // dropped — object disappeared
    };

If the object was destroyed between the get_metadata_changes call and the get_objects call, the Id is silently dropped from the created/updated arrays. This is a TOCTOU race inherent to the post-fetch design.

Trigger: any concurrent destroyer racing the /changes handler under a default-impl MetadataBackend (i.e. one that does NOT override get_metadata_changes). The MemoryBackend override does not have this issue because it pre-filters from the change log directly.

Bad behavior: the returned state token says "this is the change set for the window" but the arrays are missing entries that, at change-log time, were genuinely created/updated. A client diffing against the response will believe those objects don't exist, but the state token claims they would be included if they did. The next /changes call from the new state will not re-report them — they're just lost.

This is the wrong tradeoff at the spec layer: §3.3 says the filter applies to which entries appear, not to which entries the server is allowed to forget. The correct fallback when the post-fetch can't determine related_type/type_name for an entry is to keep the Id (conservative), not drop it. Dropping silently is the worst of both worlds — wrong arrays + a state token that claims authority.

Two acceptable fixes:
1. Keep the Id when re-fetch fails (conservative). Comment explains the trade.
2. Document that the default-impl path is best-effort and not a strict §3.3 conformance. README and rustdoc both already claim default-impl is non-strict for destroyed only — extend that caveat to created/updated, OR keep the Id.

Option 1 is the lower-surprise choice. Option 2 is honest but the gap between "strict §3.3 (override)" and "silent data loss (default)" is operationally too wide.

Recommend option 1 — flip the drop branch from  to  so disappeared-object Ids survive the filter pass. Add a regression test that simulates a between-fetch destroy and asserts the Id stays in created.

Maintainer cost if left: a contributor adding a fancier post-filter (e.g. matching on isPrivate) will copy the drop pattern and silently break a different invariant. The drop-on-failure idiom is a class of bug, not a one-off.
title: filter_changes_array silently drops Ids whose objects disappeared between /changes and re-fetch
